 Perez said the incoming mayor’s plan to cancel the Flock cameras did not contribute to his decision to leave
 Print this Article 
 View Comments Providence Police Chief Colonel Oscar Perez (right), with Rhode Island Governor Dan McKee (left) and Providence Mayor Brett Smiley, addressed reporters during the manhunt for a gunman after the Brown University mass shooting in December 2025. MARK STOCKWELL FOR THE BOSTON GLOBE PROVIDENCE — Police Chief Oscar Perez will leave his post leading the police department when Mayor-elect David Morales takes over in January. 
 “Colonel Oscar Perez has informed me that he plans to leave the department to spend time with his wife and focus on her care as she faces serious health challenges,” Morales said Tuesday morning. 
 Morales, who defeated Mayor Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary in September and easily won the general election in November, had asked Perez to stay on when he becomes mayor in January. He told the Globe earlier this month that he was optimistic Perez accept. But Perez, a longtime Providence police officer who had been appointed chief by Smiley, instead said he would retire. 
 “I respect his decision to put his family first, and I’m grateful for his decision to put his family first,” Morales said Tuesday. 
 Get Rhode Map A weekday briefing from veteran Rhode Island reporters, focused on the things that matter most in the Ocean State. Enter Email Sign Up Speaking to reporters Tuesday afternoon, Perez called the decision “bittersweet.” A Colombian immigrant who moved to Providence as a teenager, Perez was the city’s first Latino police chief when he was appointed in 2023. He has been a Providence police officer since 1994. 
 “I never thought for one second on May 13 of 1994 that I was going to be the chief of this great police department,” Perez said. “My family has taken a back seat for years, and I think it’s time that I give back to them to make sure that we enjoy our lives.” 
 His exit means police chief will be added to the long list of top jobs to fill in Providence, which also needs a new fire chief and school superintenden t. 
 Morales’s relationship with the police department could get off to a rocky start, as he’s promised to cancel the city’s contract with Flock , a company that makes license plate-reading cameras that police say have been vital in helping solve crimes. 
 Providence Chief of Police Colonel Oscar Perez sat inside the Real Time Crime Center room at the Providence Police Department on Aug. 19, 2025.
 Ben Pennington/for The Boston Globe The cameras have prompted privacy concerns, as police officers across the country have been accused of misusing the technology. 
 Perez insisted no such issues had occurred in Providence, and was hoping to convince Morales and City Council members to keep the technology. The council is currently considering an ordinance to ban it entirely. 
 Perez told the Globe last month the Flock issue would not be the deciding factor in whether he would stay on. But he sought to educate officials on how the technology has helped detectives track down suspects. 
 “I’m going to let the election process get through,” Perez said earlier this month, when asked if he would accept Morales’s offer to remain chief. “I’m just concentrating on making sure that this city is safe.” 
 More than 100 officers, including Perez, are eligible for full retirement if they choose to leave the department. Fire chief Derek Silva also announced last week he would retire. In addition to filling those two jobs, Morales also wants to hire a public safety commissioner, which would oversee both departments. 
 The police union campaigned against Morales during the election, criticizing his previous position on defunding police and his current calls to abolish ICE . 
 Morales has repeatedly said he no longer wants to decrease funding to the police department. 
 In a statement Tuesday, Morales said he is “committed to ensuring that our Providence Police Department has the resources, support and strong, steady leadership our officers need to serve our communities effectively and keep our neighborhoods safe.” 
 June Rose, the executive director of Morales’s transition, said both internal and external candidates for chief would be considered. 
 Perez quickly endorsed deputy chief Timothy O’Hara for the job, who he said has “been through the trenches with me.” 
 “He’s ready to take the role,” Perez said. 
 Smiley praised Perez for his 32 years with the department on Tuesday. 
 “Under his leadership, Providence has experienced historic reductions in crime, became a national model in community policing and made significant investments in public safety,” Smiley said. “I am forever grateful for his partnership, his steady leadership during some of our city’s most challenging moments and his unwavering commitment to the people of Providence.” 
 Perez’s last day is Jan. 4, 2027.
